Shadow AI agents are multiplying. Here's how to find and secure them.

Nudge Security says unmanaged “shadow” AI agents are spreading across workplace tools with persistent access to corporate apps and data, creating governance risks that traditional app discovery can miss. Its sponsored pitch is that combining API-based and browser-based discovery can inventory these agents, assess risky permissions or configurations, and help security teams assign owners and enforce oversight.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The article says employees are building AI agents in platforms such as Salesforce Agentforce, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Cursor, Zapier, and Retool, often without visibility or approval from IT or security teams.
  • 02The article argues that shadow AI agents are riskier than shadow AI apps because agents hold persistent permissions, connect to corporate apps and data, and can take actions on their own.
  • 03Nudge Security says it provides an immediate inventory of AI agents across platforms including Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude Managed Agents, Tines, ServiceNow, Salesforce Agentforce, and Cursor Automations.
  • 04Nudge Security describes using both API-based discovery and browser-based discovery to find agents on platforms that either expose agent data through public APIs or do not expose such data through APIs.
  • 05The article says Nudge Security can surface risks such as publicly accessible agents, excessive or destructive permissions, hardcoded credentials or PII in instructions, unauthenticated MCP connections, dormant agents with active access, and agents whose creators have left the organization.

The article says employees are creating AI agents in tools such as Salesforce Agentforce, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Cursor, Zapier, Retool, and other platforms, often without visibility or approval from IT or security teams. It argues that the business has already adopted these agents “one shadow agent at a time,” leaving security teams to identify who built them, what they can access, and what actions they can take. The article presents Nudge Security as a product for discovering, assessing, and governing these AI agents.

The article says shadow AI agents are riskier than shadow AI apps because agents can hold persistent permissions, connect to corporate applications and data, and take actions without waiting for a user to send a prompt. It cites figures saying 48% of cybersecurity professionals rank agentic AI as the most dangerous attack vector of 2026, 80% of organizations have encountered agentic AI risks, and only 21% of IT leaders have a mature agentic AI governance program. It frames the gap between agent exposure and governance readiness as the area where unmanaged AI agents create risk.

Nudge Security says it uses API-based discovery for platforms that expose agent data, including Salesforce Agentforce, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Google Gemini, ServiceNow, n8n, Tines, ChatGPT, Abacus.AI, and Workato. It also describes browser-based discovery through its browser extension for platforms that do not expose agent details through APIs, including Cursor automations, OpenAI Agent Workflows, ChatGPT workspace agents, Zoom AI Workflows, Atlassian Rovo, Retool, Zapier Agents, and HyperAgent. For discovered agents, the article says Nudge Security can surface risks such as public accessibility, excessive or destructive permissions, hardcoded credentials or PII in instructions, unauthenticated MCP connections, dormant agents with active access, and agents whose creators have left the organization.

  • The article highlights that relying only on platform APIs can miss a large portion of agent activity because many tools where employees build agents either do not offer APIs or do not expose agent details through them.
  • Browser-based discovery is presented as important because it can detect agents at the moment an employee views, lists, or creates them on platforms that lack usable API visibility.
  • The article frames the highest-risk shadow agents as potentially coming from low-friction tools used by engineers, operations teams, and product managers because those tools are easy to adopt without IT approval and may still connect to sensitive systems.
  • A practical governance step described in the article is to assign an accountable owner for each discovered agent, which may be different from the original creator, so responsibility remains clear after discovery.
  • The article identifies departed creators as a specific agent risk, meaning organizations should check not only what an agent can access but also whether the person who built it is still with the company.

Employees are creating AI agents in tools like Salesforce Agentforce, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Cursor, Zapier, and others, often without IT or security teams knowing about them. This matters because these agents can keep access to company apps and data and can take actions on their own, so a hidden or poorly set up agent could touch important systems without oversight. The article says Nudge Security helps organizations find these agents, see what they can access, spot risky settings, and assign someone to manage them.

The ShinyHunters extortion gang has claimed responsibility for a recently disclosed Ernst & Young data breach. EY previously said a third-party information technology service management platform used by its IT personnel was compromised. Support tickets submitted through the platform may include documents containing client tax information, and EY said multiple documents were downloaded.

EY detected unusual activity on April 23 and determined that the attacker accessed the platform between March 28 and April 12. ShinyHunters claimed to BleepingComputer that EY credentials were obtained through a supply-chain attack and used to access EY’s Jira, GitHub, and Azure environments. BleepingComputer said it could not independently verify the threat actor’s claims, and EY has not confirmed that ShinyHunters was behind the attack.

The stolen documents contained personal and financial information included in or used to prepare tax filings, according to EY’s notification. The company has not disclosed the name of the compromised support system, the specific types of information exposed, or how many people were affected. EY said it secured its systems, removed the unauthorized access, notified federal law enforcement, and is offering affected clients 24 months of identity monitoring and restoration services through Experian.

  • The breach involved a support ticket platform used for IT help with tax-related work, showing that sensitive client tax documents can be exposed through routine support workflows rather than only through primary tax systems.
  • EY’s public notice confirms stolen documents but omits the support system name, exposed data types, and affected population size, leaving clients without several details needed to judge their personal risk.
  • The attacker’s claimed access went beyond the acknowledged support-ticket compromise to Jira, GitHub, and Azure environments, but the article emphasizes that BleepingComputer could not verify those broader claims and EY had not confirmed them.
  • Affected clients are being offered 24 months of Experian identity monitoring and restoration services, indicating EY considers the stolen tax-related documents sensitive enough to warrant identity-protection support.

Ernst & Young says someone broke into a third-party support ticket system used by its IT staff and downloaded documents from tickets that may include clients’ tax information. The ShinyHunters group now claims it was responsible and says it got EY login details through another company, then used them to access EY systems such as Jira, GitHub, and Azure, though EY has not confirmed that claim. People whose information was in the stolen documents could have personal and financial details exposed, and EY is offering affected clients 24 months of identity monitoring and restoration services.

New Certighost PoC exploit lets attackers hijack Windows domains

A public proof-of-concept exploit for the Certighost AD CS flaw can let an authenticated low-privileged Windows domain user obtain a certificate as a domain controller and potentially compromise the entire domain. Microsoft patched the issue in July 2026, and admins should apply the updates or temporarily disable the vulnerable chase fallback.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A proof-of-concept exploit for the Certighost Windows Active Directory Certificate Services vulnerability has been released and can allow authenticated attackers to potentially compromise a Windows domain.
  • 02Microsoft tracked the vulnerability as CVE-2026-54121 and fixed it in the July 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates.
  • 03The vulnerability allowed attackers to direct the Certification Authority to attacker-controlled services because systems did not verify that the server supplied through the cdc value was a legitimate domain controller.
  • 04The released certighost.py proof-of-concept automates the process of using a certificate to authenticate through PKINIT as a targeted domain controller, saving Kerberos credentials to a .ccache file and extracting the account’s NT hash.
  • 05Microsoft’s fix adds validation so the Certification Authority verifies that the cdc server maps to a legitimate domain controller in Active Directory and confirms that the returned identity matches the expected account.

A proof-of-concept exploit has been released for “Certighost,” a Windows Active Directory Certificate Services vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-54121. Microsoft fixed the flaw in the July 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates after it was reported by researchers H0j3n and Aniq Fakhrul on May 14, 2026. The article says authenticated attackers could potentially compromise a Windows domain by obtaining a certificate that allows authentication as a machine account via PKINIT.

The researchers said Certighost allowed a low-privileged domain user to impersonate a Domain Controller and achieve domain compromise in the tested AD CS configuration. The issue involved an AD CS fallback mechanism called a “chase,” where attacker-controlled certificate request values could direct the Certification Authority to a supplied server and account search target. Systems previously did not verify that the supplied server was a legitimate domain controller, allowing attackers to run rogue SMB, LSA, and LDAP services and return false directory information.

The released certighost.py proof-of-concept automates the attack by using the certificate to authenticate through PKINIT as a targeted domain controller, saving Kerberos credentials to a .ccache file and extracting the account’s NT hash. The researchers demonstrated using those Kerberos credentials with Impacket’s secretsdump tool to perform a DCSync attack and retrieve the krbtgt account’s credentials. Microsoft’s fix validates that the cdc server maps to a legitimate domain controller and that the returned identity matches the expected account, while the researchers also provided a temporary workaround to disable the optional chase fallback for admins who cannot install the updates.

  • The attack can begin with a low-privileged user creating a machine account, which the article says is allowed under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota configuration.
  • The vulnerable “chase” fallback trusted identity information from attacker-controlled SMB, LSA, and LDAP services because it did not verify that the supplied server was a legitimate domain controller.
  • A successful attack against a domain controller account can be escalated into a DCSync attack because domain controller accounts have directory replication rights.
  • Administrators who cannot immediately install the July 2026 updates can temporarily disable the optional chase fallback with certutil, but the researchers warned that this mitigation has not been fully tested in production environments.

Researchers released a working example showing how a regular signed-in Windows domain user could abuse a flaw in Microsoft’s certificate system for company networks. If the target is a domain controller, the attacker could pretend to be that central server and gain powerful control over the whole Windows domain. Microsoft fixed the flaw in its July 2026 updates, and organizations that use Active Directory Certificate Services are the ones affected.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific, high-impact finding affecting Microsoft Active Directory Certificate Services, with a public proof-of-concept that can potentially enable Windows domain compromise. Although the article does not report active exploitation in the wild, the combination of domain-level impact, public exploit code, and available patch makes it highly relevant for security professionals.

Hackers target US firms in FastJson RCE zero-day attacks

Hackers are actively exploiting a critical FastJson 1.x zero-day (CVE-2026-16723) to achieve remote code execution against mostly U.S. organizations, especially Spring Boot fat-JAR deployments. No patch is available, so affected users should enable SafeMode or move to an unaffected version such as fastjson2.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-16723, a remote code execution vulnerability in the FastJson open-source Java library that requires no user interaction or elevated privileges.
  • 02The vulnerability affects FastJson versions 1.2.68 through 1.2.83 and is being used in attacks targeting a wide range of mostly U.S.-based organizations, with some attacks in Singapore and Canada.
  • 03Imperva said the attacks target organizations across Financial Services, Healthcare, Computing, Retail, Business, and other industries.
  • 04Alibaba said the issue is exploitable in the common Spring Boot executable fat-JAR deployment model and that specifying a target class during deserialization does not mitigate the vulnerability.
  • 05There is currently no fix for CVE-2026-16723, and developers using affected versions are urged to enable SafeMode immediately or switch to a non-impacted build.

Hackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-16723, a remote code execution vulnerability in the FastJson open-source Java library. The issue affects FastJson versions 1.2.68 through 1.2.83 and can be exploited without user interaction or elevated privileges. ThreatBook observed the malicious activity last week, and Imperva said attacks are targeting a wide range of organizations, mostly in the United States, with some activity in Singapore and Canada.

FastJson is an Alibaba-developed Java library used to serialize Java objects to JSON and deserialize JSON back into Java objects. FearsOff discovered the vulnerability and published a technical write-up explaining that the flaw comes from the library’s type-resolution logic, which performs attacker-controlled resource lookups before enforcing AutoType restrictions. The researchers said this allows malicious classes to be loaded and executed in Spring Boot fat-JAR deployments without AutoType enabled or third-party gadget chains.

Alibaba confirmed the vulnerability’s critical severity and said it is exploitable in the common Spring Boot executable fat-JAR deployment model. The vendor said specifying a target class during deserialization does not mitigate the issue because attackers can embed malicious payloads in Object or Map fields. There is currently no fix for CVE-2026-16723, and developers using affected versions are urged to enable SafeMode or switch to a non-impacted build.

  • FastJson 1.2.60 and earlier are not affected, so upgrading is not the only possible version-change path; moving to a non-impacted build is also cited as mitigation.
  • The flaw can be exploited even when AutoType is not enabled and without third-party gadget chains, which weakens assumptions that those conditions would prevent this class of issue.
  • Specifying a target class during deserialization is explicitly not a mitigation because attackers can place malicious payloads inside Object or Map fields.
  • The vulnerable type-resolution logic is absent from fastjson2, which uses an allowlist-first model for polymorphic deserialization, making migration to fastjson2 a more durable remediation path than waiting for a FastJson 1.x patch.

Hackers are using a newly reported weakness in FastJson, a widely used Java tool from Alibaba that helps software handle JSON data, to make targeted systems run their code without anyone clicking anything. The affected versions are FastJson 1.2.68 through 1.2.83, mainly when used in common Spring Boot applications packaged as executable files, and attacks are mostly hitting U.S. organizations in finance, healthcare, computing, retail, business, and other sectors. This matters because there is currently no fix for the issue, FastJson 1.x is no longer actively maintained, and the attacks are expected to spread beyond the current countries mentioned.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a must-read because it reports active exploitation of a critical FastJson remote code execution zero-day affecting versions 1.2.68 through 1.2.83, with no fix currently available. The issue has broad relevance because attacks are targeting multiple industries, mostly in the United States, and the vulnerable library is widely used in Java software.

New Dysphoria DDoS botnet spreads to 200k devices worldwide

The Dysphoria botnet has infected about 200,000 routers, cameras, and other IoT devices worldwide, using blockchain-based command-and-control to make takedown harder. It is being used for DDoS attacks and proxy relay operations, spreading through weak credentials and known device vulnerabilities.
KEY POINTS
  • 01QiAnXin XLab researchers estimate that the Dysphoria botnet has compromised around 200,000 devices worldwide and is being used for DDoS attacks and traffic relay operations.
  • 02Dysphoria evolved from the jackskid and fbot malware by adding a blockchain-based command-and-control resolution mechanism that uses Ethereum ENS and Solana SNS domains.
  • 03XLab observed Dysphoria variants that added features such as a C2 acquisition algorithm, multi-chain support, new domains, and separation between relaying and DDoS functions.
  • 04The botnet spreads through weak Telnet and SSH credentials and known vulnerabilities in routers, cameras, and various IoT devices, including several recent and older CVEs.
  • 05Dysphoria’s operators claim a maximum DDoS capacity of 4 Tbps on a clearnet site that promotes the service as a legitimate stress-tester.

A botnet called Dysphoria has compromised around 200,000 devices worldwide and is using them for distributed denial of service attacks and traffic relay operations. QiAnXin XLab researchers say the botnet evolved from the jackskid and fbot malware families. They first spotted Dysphoria on March 25 and observed multiple iterations that added meaningful updates over the following months.

Dysphoria uses a covert blockchain-based command-and-control resolution mechanism that relies on Ethereum ENS and Solana SNS domains to retrieve infrastructure information. Its command-and-control addresses are concealed inside fake IPv6 strings and recovered using a custom byte-transformation algorithm. XLab said this use of blockchain makes the botnet’s infrastructure harder to trace and dismantle.

The botnet spreads through weak Telnet and SSH credentials and known vulnerabilities in routers, cameras, and various IoT devices. XLab observed a late-June variant that focused only on turning infected devices into network proxies and discarded DDoS functionality, using UPnP to create 155 port forwarding rules. The operators claim a maximum DDoS capacity of 4 Tbps, while the article notes users can reduce infection risk by updating firmware, changing default administrator passwords, disabling unnecessary remote access, and strengthening available security settings.

  • Dysphoria’s use of Ethereum ENS and Solana SNS for command-and-control resolution makes its infrastructure harder to trace and dismantle than a botnet relying only on conventional domains or IP addresses.
  • The late-June variant that removed DDoS functionality and focused only on proxying shows the same infected device pool can be repurposed for different criminal infrastructure needs.
  • The botnet’s exploitation of both recent flaws and older issues such as CVE-2017-17215 and CVE-2020-8515 shows that long-unpatched routers and IoT devices remain valuable targets years after vulnerabilities are disclosed.
  • Because Dysphoria spreads through weak Telnet and SSH credentials as well as known device flaws, changing default administrator passwords and disabling unnecessary remote access are directly relevant defenses mentioned in the article.

A malicious network called Dysphoria has taken over about 200,000 devices around the world, including routers, cameras, and other internet-connected equipment. The people behind it use those devices to overwhelm websites or online services with traffic and to pass internet traffic through infected devices, making the activity harder to trace. This matters because even ordinary home or business devices with weak passwords or old software can be pulled into attacks that disrupt services for others.

Apple sued over fake App Store crypto wallet app stealing $1.8M in Bitcoin

Apple is being sued after three users allegedly lost about $1.8 million in Bitcoin to a fake Sparrow Wallet app downloaded from the App Store. The lawsuit claims Apple failed to properly vet and remove the fraudulent app despite prior warnings, while presenting the App Store as a trusted marketplace.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Three plaintiffs sued Apple in California, alleging they lost approximately $1.8 million in Bitcoin after downloading and using a fraudulent Sparrow Wallet application from the App Store.
  • 02The complaint says the fake app impersonated the legitimate Sparrow Bitcoin wallet and instructed users to enter their seed phrases, after which their Bitcoin was transferred to wallets controlled by scammers.
  • 03The legitimate Sparrow Wallet is a desktop application for Windows, macOS, and Linux and does not offer an iOS version.
  • 04The lawsuit alleges Apple ranked the fraudulent Sparrow app and included it in curated cryptocurrency app collections, effectively recommending it alongside legitimate applications.
  • 05Apple told BleepingComputer that it acted quickly to remove applications impersonating Sparrow Wallet and terminated the developer accounts associated with them.

Apple is being sued by three people who claim they lost approximately $1.8 million in Bitcoin after downloading and using a fraudulent Sparrow Wallet application from the App Store. The complaint, filed on July 24 in California, alleges that Apple failed to adequately review and monitor apps distributed through the App Store while promoting it as a safe and trusted source for software. Plaintiffs James Ramirez, Christopher Ellis, and Jalen Delgado say the malicious app impersonated the legitimate Sparrow Bitcoin wallet and instructed them to enter their seed phrases.

After the plaintiffs entered those secret recovery credentials, their Bitcoin was allegedly transferred to cryptocurrency wallets controlled by scammers. The legitimate Sparrow Wallet is a desktop application for Windows, macOS, and Linux and does not offer an iOS version. The complaint says Delgado lost about \(120,000, Ramirez lost about \)875,000, and Ellis lost about $840,000 after using the fraudulent app.

The lawsuit claims Apple ranked the fraudulent Sparrow app and included it in curated cryptocurrency app collections, effectively recommending it alongside legitimate applications. It also says Apple had been warned about fraudulent Sparrow Wallet apps more than a year before the plaintiffs’ losses, citing warnings from Sparrow Wallet developer Craig Raw. Apple told BleepingComputer that it acted quickly to remove apps impersonating Sparrow Wallet, terminated associated developer accounts, and provides ways for developers and customers to report infringement, scams, and fraud.

  • The legitimate Sparrow Wallet has no iOS version, so any mobile app using the Sparrow Wallet name in Apple’s App Store was inherently suspect according to the article.
  • The complaint says one plaintiff reported the fake app to Apple on July 25, 2025, but another plaintiff allegedly downloaded the same app and lost funds just over a week later, making Apple’s response time a central issue in the lawsuit.
  • Sparrow Wallet’s developer had publicly warned about fake App Store versions more than a year before the plaintiffs’ alleged losses, suggesting the impersonation problem was not limited to a single short-lived app listing.
  • The article highlights that App Store placement can amplify risk because the complaint alleges Apple ranked the fraudulent app and included it in curated cryptocurrency app collections.

Three people say they lost about $1.8 million in Bitcoin after downloading a fake Sparrow Wallet app from Apple’s App Store and entering the secret recovery words that let the scammers move their funds. They are suing Apple, arguing that the company did not properly check or remove the fake app even though similar scams had reportedly been warned about before. The case matters because many people trust app stores to be safe, and the lawsuit challenges whether Apple should be responsible when a fake financial app in its store causes major losses.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific incident involving alleged cryptocurrency theft through a fraudulent App Store wallet app and a lawsuit against Apple, with useful lessons about app impersonation and seed phrase theft. It is relevant to security professionals, especially those focused on fraud, mobile app ecosystems, or crypto-related abuse, but it is not an active exploitation alert, critical patch, or major enterprise breach.

Arista patches VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day exploited in attacks

Arista has patched a maximum-severity unauthenticated command injection zero-day in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator that is already being exploited. Administrators should upgrade immediately, restrict web interface access, and check logs for compromise indicators.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Arista patched CVE-2026-16812, a maximum-severity unauthenticated OS command injection vulnerability in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments that is being actively exploited.
  • 02The vulnerability allows remote attackers with network access to the VCO web interface to access privileged functionality without VCO tenant or operator credentials.

Arista has patched CVE-2026-16812, a maximum-severity unauthenticated OS command injection vulnerability in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments. The flaw is being actively exploited in attacks and has a severity score of 10.0. VeloCloud Orchestrator is a centralized management platform used to configure, monitor, and manage VeloCloud SD-WAN deployments and associated edge devices.

According to Arista, attackers only need network access to the VCO web interface and do not need VCO tenant or operator credentials. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the orchestrator and the data it manages, and Arista warns that attackers could also gain access to VeloCloud Edge devices. GitHub has announced a new cooldown mechanism in Dependabot that allows the tool to wait at least three days after a release is published before opening a pull request. The default three-day cooldown applies only to version updates, which are used to keep software dependencies up to date. Security updates will still be pushed immediately, allowing Dependabot to issue an alert and open a pull request to move a project to a patched version.

GitHub said the change is meant to reduce the risk from poisoned versions of popular packages that may be published by threat actors and quickly pulled into downstream projects before being removed from a registry. The company described three days as a balance between getting past the window where most of these attacks occur and not delaying dependency updates longer than necessary. It also said the cooldown setting in dependabot.yml can still be configured differently to fit a project’s needs.

GitHub emphasized that the cooldown should be only one layer of defense alongside measures such as pinning dependencies with lockfiles, disabling install scripts in CI, scoping build pipeline tokens, and reviewing updates before they merge. The company noted that cooldowns are designed for short-lived malicious releases and do little against longer-running threats such as dormant backdoors, maintainer sabotage, or compromised build systems. The article also notes that similar cooldown controls have appeared across VS Code, Ruby, Bun, npm, pnpm, and Yarn, while PyPI plans to block adding new files to package releases after 14 days.

  • GitHub’s choice of a three-day default is explicitly meant to outlast the period in which most short-lived poisoned package attacks are detected, without delaying routine dependency updates longer than necessary.
  • The cooldown does not protect against slower or more persistent supply-chain threats such as dormant backdoors, maintainer sabotage, or compromised build systems, so it is targeted at only one attack pattern.
  • GitHub is preserving immediate Dependabot security updates, showing that the new delay is designed to reduce risky routine upgrades without slowing fixes for known security issues.
  • The article indicates a broader ecosystem shift toward time-based defenses, with similar cooldown or release-locking measures appearing across VS Code, Ruby, Bun, npm, pnpm, Yarn, and PyPI.

GitHub is changing Dependabot so it normally waits at least three days before suggesting routine software dependency updates, instead of immediately pulling in a brand-new release. The delay matters because attackers can sometimes publish a poisoned version of a popular package, and even if it is removed quickly, fast automatic updates can spread it to many projects before anyone catches it. Security fixes will still be sent right away, and GitHub says this delay is only one safety layer, not a complete defense.

Victims are directed through compromised web infrastructure to a fake Microsoft Store page claiming that Microsoft Teams must be updated before a shared document can be opened. ZeroBEC attributed the campaign with moderate-to-high confidence to a threat actor group operating from Nigeria based on infrastructure, code history, and a GitHub environment used to run the campaigns.

Researchers said installing multiple RMM tools on the same host appears intended to create redundant access and improve resilience if one tool is detected and removed.

After deployment, the threat actors were observed running commands to check system state, volume protection, firewall profiles, local Administrators group membership, and the local Administrators group name. n8n patched a high-severity expression-sandbox escape that could let an authenticated workflow editor execute operating-system commands on the server running the automation platform. The affected ranges are <2.31.5 and >=2.32.0,<2.32.1, and the flaw was fixed in versions 2.31.5 and 2.32.1. The issue is tracked as GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m, rated High with a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.7, and had no CVE assigned as of July 27, 2026.

Exploitation requires a valid account with permission to create or modify workflows and does not require action from another user. A successful exploit runs commands with the privileges of the n8n process. Security Joes said this access could expose N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY, allow decryption of credentials stored in n8n, and open paths to connected databases, internal services, and cloud endpoints.

Security Joes found the flaw while probing n8n’s February fix for CVE-2026-27577 for another bypass. The researchers said the escape involved a gap in handling ArrowFunctionExpression and a blind spot in property checks involving Reflect.get(), which they used to recover process.getBuiltinModule, load child_process, and run a command on the host. Administrators are advised to update rather than rely on interim access restrictions, and defenders should review recent workflows and hunt for suspicious child processes spawned by n8n or Node.js.

  • The public advisory lists no patched 1.x release and does not say whether n8n Cloud was affected, leaving some deployment questions unanswered.
  • Defenders have concrete post-upgrade hunting leads from the article, including unexpected arrow functions or obfuscated JavaScript in workflows and command-line tools spawned by the n8n or Node.js process.

n8n fixed a serious flaw that could let someone with an account allowed to create or change workflows make the server run computer commands. This affects organizations using vulnerable n8n versions before 2.31.5 or 2.32.1, especially if those systems store important login details or can reach internal services. In the real world, a stolen or misused workflow-editing account could expose stored credentials and give an attacker access to databases, cloud services, or other systems the n8n server can reach.

Public exploit details released on July 27 show how an unauthenticated request can reach PHP’s eval() function inside vBulletin and execute code on an unpatched forum server. The attack requires no account, administrative access, or interaction from another user. SSD Secure Disclosure lists vBulletin 6.2.1 and earlier, and 6.1.6 and earlier, as affected, while vBulletin issued patches for 6.2.1, 6.2.0, and 6.1.6 at the end of June and released fixed version 6.2.2 on July 1.

The issue is identified as CVE-2026-61511, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in vBulletin’s template engine. The vulnerable code sits in /includes/vb5/template/runtime.php, inside the vB5_Template_Runtime::runMaths() method, which strips characters outside a restricted set and then passes what remains directly to eval(). vBulletin renders templates over the public ajax/render/pagenav route, and the stock pagenav template copies a visitor-supplied pagenav[pagenumber] value into a {vb:math} tag that reaches runMaths().

Administrators running self-hosted installations should apply the patch for their branch or upgrade to 6.2.2, while vBulletin says its Cloud sites have already been patched. SSD did not report active exploitation, and as of July 27, 2026, no source had confirmed in-the-wild attacks or listed CVE-2026-61511 in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The published proof-of-concept contains a one-character error that stops it from running unchanged, but the article says the mistake is trivial to correct and does not affect the underlying vulnerability.

  • The published proof-of-concept contains a one-character typo that prevents it from running unchanged, but the article says the mistake is trivial to fix and does not reduce the underlying risk.
  • Defenders can look for POST requests with routestring=ajax/render/pagenav and unusually long or operator-heavy pagenav[pagenumber] values, a detection pattern derived from the public proof-of-concept.
  • The article highlights an unresolved exposure window between the late-June patch and the July 27 exploit disclosure, because neither SSD nor vBulletin said whether the flaw had been used during that period.
  • The vulnerability follows a pattern seen in prior vBulletin template-engine issues, where quiet fixes are followed later by working public exploits while many internet-facing forums remain unpatched.

This matters because internet-facing forums that miss these quiet fixes can remain open to takeover once working examples become public.

NVIDIA and 36 partners launched the Open Secure AI Alliance to promote open tools and locally run AI models for securing AI agents, with NVIDIA’s NOOA framework as the first code release. NVIDIA and 36 other organizations formed the Open Secure AI Alliance to develop and share open technologies, techniques, and tools for securing software and AI agents. The 37-member group includes Microsoft, Cisco, Cloudflare, CrowdStrike, Hugging Face, IBM, Palo Alto Networks, Red Hat, and the Linux Foundation. Its stated scope covers the full agent stack, including identity, permissions, isolation, guardrails, logs, model formats, multi-model scanning, and secure coding workflows.

The launch includes NVIDIA-labs OO Agents, or NOOA, an Apache 2.0 research framework intended to make agent behavior easier to test, trace, audit, and govern. NOOA represents an agent harness as a Python class, where fields store state, methods expose capabilities, docstrings act as prompts, and type annotations define contracts the model must follow. NVIDIA reported that NOOA scored 86.8% on the CyberGym L1 vulnerability-rediscovery benchmark using GPT-5.5, with network access blocked and rule-based checks applied to each trajectory.

The article emphasizes that NOOA can be configured to execute LLM-generated Python, which may transmit private data, delete files, or modify its environment. NVIDIA says NOOA’s checks and deny-lists are not a containment boundary, and agents executing generated code must run behind operating system-level isolation such as a container, virtual machine, or OpenShell sandbox. The alliance’s public materials do not yet include a charter, governing board, technical workstreams, delivery schedule, shared repository, governance model, joint roadmap, or first multi-member deliverable.

  • NOOA’s own documentation treats its Python checks and module deny-lists as insufficient for containment, so any agent that executes generated code must be run behind operating-system isolation such as a container, virtual machine, or OpenShell sandbox.
  • The Hugging Face case supports the value of locally run models for incident reconstruction, but the article says it does not show that the open model detected, stopped, or contained the breach.
  • Commercially hosted frontier-model APIs initially rejected the attack commands, exploit payloads, and command-and-control artifacts Hugging Face needed for its forensic analysis, which made local control of a capable model operationally important.
  • Several technologies cited in the alliance announcement, including Safetensors, SPIFFE/SPIRE, Lightwell, MDASH, and Grok Build, already existed before the coalition, so the public record does not yet show them as alliance-created products.
  • The alliance has a large membership list but no public charter, governance model, workstreams, shared repository, roadmap, or first multi-member deliverable, making the depth of member participation hard to assess.

NVIDIA and 36 other organizations have formed the Open Secure AI Alliance to build and share tools for making AI agents safer, and NVIDIA released an early open-source framework called NOOA for testing and tracing what those agents do. This matters because companies such as Hugging Face have already dealt with an AI-related intrusion, and the article says defenders may need AI systems they can run on their own computers during an emergency rather than relying only on outside services. The affected groups include AI companies, cloud and security vendors, and organizations that may use AI agents, but the alliance has not yet publicly explained its rules, roadmap, or what all members will actually contribute.

Azure VM Command Execution using Third-Party Extensions – Salt Minion

An attacker with Azure VM extension write permissions can abuse the legitimate Salt Minion third-party extension to connect a VM to a rogue Salt master and execute commands as root or SYSTEM. Organizations should tightly restrict extension write privileges and monitor Azure Activity Logs and endpoint process activity for Salt Minion installation and command execution.
KEY POINTS
  • 01An attacker with Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write permission can deploy the Salt Minion Azure VM extension and configure it to connect to a rogue Salt Master.
  • 02After the Salt Minion connects and its key is accepted, the rogue Salt Master can push Salt states or run commands directly on the target VM as root on Linux.
  • 03The article demonstrates using a malicious Salt state to retrieve an Azure Managed Identity access token from the VM metadata service and send it to an out-of-band interaction endpoint.
  • 04Azure Activity Log monitoring for Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write can detect installation of the salt-minion.linux or salt-minion.windows extension.
  • 05On Linux, Salt minion logs, auditd records, and process-tree data can show cmd.run activity and root command execution originating from Salt Minion, while on Windows process events can show Salt Minion spawning cmd.exe.

This article explains how Azure VM command execution can be achieved by abusing the legitimate third-party Salt Minion extension. An attacker with Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write permission can deploy the Salt Minion extension to a target Azure virtual machine and point it at a rogue Salt Master they control. After the minion connects and its key is accepted, the attacker can push Salt states or run commands on the VM.

The article demonstrates creating a malicious Salt state that retrieves an Azure Managed Identity access token from the VM metadata service and posts it to an out-of-band interaction endpoint. On Linux, the demonstrated command execution runs as root, and the article also notes that arbitrary commands can be run directly through Salt without sending a new state. The technique applies to both Linux and Windows Azure VMs using the salt-minion.linux or salt-minion.windows extension.

The significance is that several built-in and less commonly discussed Azure roles have the extension write permission needed to perform this activity, including Owner, Contributor, Log Analytics Contributor, Virtual Machine Contributor, and others. The article recommends monitoring Azure Activity Logs for VM extension write operations and specifically for Salt Minion extension installation. It also describes Linux detection opportunities through Salt logs, auditd, and process-tree context, while Windows detection relies on process events showing Salt Minion spawning system command processes.

  • The Salt Minion approach is described as simpler than the Chef extension approach because it does not require licensing, cookbook infrastructure, or validation keys.
  • The article highlights several less obvious Azure roles with VM extension write permissions, such as Log Analytics Contributor, VM Restore Operator, and Defender-related server roles, expanding the set of identities that may effectively be able to execute code on VMs.
  • If a sensitive system such as a domain controller is deployed as an Azure VM, anyone who can write extensions to it is effectively a domain administrator according to the article.
  • Auditd alone can show that commands ran as root without an interactive login session, but process-tree context from tools like pspy or EDR is needed to connect that activity back to Salt Minion.
  • The article emphasizes that VM extensions should not be eliminated because they are important for administration, but their abuse should be addressed through tighter permissions and detection around sensitive actions.

The article explains how someone with permission to add software add-ons to an Azure virtual machine could install a legitimate Salt Minion add-on and point it to a server they control, letting them run commands on that machine. This affects organizations that use Azure virtual machines, especially sensitive ones like domain controllers, because several common Azure roles have the needed permission. The broader risk is that normal-looking administration features can be misused to gain powerful access, so organizations need to limit who can use them and watch for signs of this activity.

The PDF That Scanned Clean Because Nobody Could Read It

A phishing email used a password-protected PDF with an obfuscated link hidden in a PDF annotation so attachment scanners could not inspect it and returned a clean verdict. The attack was still detected by behavioral and authentication signals, including SPF/DKIM/DMARC failures, sender-domain mismatches, and first-time sender indicators.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A fake payroll remittance notification delivered a password-protected PDF, with the password supplied in the email body.
  • 02The malicious link inside the PDF was stored as a hex-encoded value in a PDF annotation rather than as visible text.
  • 03The attachment scanner returned a clean verdict because it could not parse the encrypted PDF and could not extract the hidden link.
  • 04The message was ultimately classified as phishing based on authentication failures, a mismatch between the visible sender and DKIM-signing domain, first-time sender status, and branding inconsistencies.
  • 05The article advises defenders to treat unexpected password-protected documents, especially payroll or payment-related files with passwords in the email body, as suspicious.

A fake payroll remittance notification targeted a VP of Human Resources at a mid-size manufacturer and then propagated to two more mailboxes before it was mitigated. The email delivered a password-protected PDF, with the password supplied in the email body and numerically linked to the filename. The attachment scanner returned a clean verdict, but the incident was still resolved as phishing.

The PDF used two evasion layers: encryption prevented tools from extracting or rendering its contents, and the link inside was hex-encoded and buried in a PDF annotation rather than shown as visible text. Static analysis did not resolve the true landing page, and the article states that the destination stayed hidden until a user opened the file and clicked. Detection instead came from the message’s wider behavior and headers, including SPF softfail, DKIM-domain and From-domain mismatch, failed DKIM verification, DMARC failure, first-time sender status, and branding mismatch.

  • A clean verdict on a password-protected attachment can indicate that the scanner was locked out rather than that the file is safe.
  • The attacker made the password and filename numerically related, which helped the password-protected PDF appear like a legitimate system-generated payroll document.
  • The email’s headers exposed the deception even though the attachment contents remained unreadable, because the visible sender, DKIM signing domain, and authenticated sending identity did not align.
  • The article emphasizes that sender authentication, first-contact behavior, branding coherence, and message intent can outweigh a static attachment verdict when the payload is deliberately unreadable.

A fake payroll email was sent to a human resources executive at a mid-size manufacturer and then reached two other mailboxes, carrying a locked PDF whose password was included in the message. Because the file was locked and the harmful link inside was hidden, the attachment check said it was safe even though the message was phishing. This matters because people in payroll, finance, and HR may be tricked by realistic work messages, and a “clean” file result can simply mean the security tool could not read what was inside.

The article analyzes a concrete phishing incident involving a password-protected PDF and hidden PDF annotation link that evaded attachment scanning. Your Employees Have One Digital Identity

The article argues that attackers target employees as whole people, linking personal accounts, devices, credentials, and corporate access into one risk surface. Enterprises should use privacy-conscious “fuzed identity” intelligence to connect those signals, prioritize real exposure, and attribute fragmented criminal personas more accurately.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The article argues that the threat boundary between enterprise identity and personal digital identity has disappeared because attackers target the whole person rather than only the corporate account.
  • 02A fuzed identity is described as an evidence-based view that links disparate identity elements to the same individual using corroborating attributes, provenance, temporal consistency, behavioral signals, and confidence scoring.
  • 03Microsoft’s June 2026 analysis of StealC and Amadey found that infostealer infections often occur outside managed enterprise networks, including on employees’ home computers that may contain corporate credentials or active session cookies.
  • 04The article says fuzed identity context can help enterprises prioritize workforce risk by distinguishing between low-risk historical credential exposure and higher-risk cases involving privileges, reused credentials, active session cookies, and newly exposed accounts.
  • 05The article emphasizes that responsible fuzed identity programs should collect only security-relevant information, document purpose, retain provenance, restrict access, establish confidence thresholds, and require human review for consequential decisions.

The article argues that enterprises can no longer treat an employee’s corporate account as separate from the person’s broader digital life. Personal email addresses, phone numbers, social profiles, devices, browser sessions, exposed credentials, and other identifiers can all become part of corporate risk. From a threat perspective, the article says the boundary between enterprise identity and personal digital identity has disappeared.

It presents “fuzed identity” as an evidence-based way to link separate identity fragments to the same person using corroborating attributes, provenance, temporal consistency, behavioral signals, and confidence scoring. The article cites Microsoft’s June 2026 analysis of StealC and Amadey to show that infostealer infections on personal devices can expose corporate credentials or active session cookies. It also references Verizon’s 2025 credential research, which found compromised credentials were an initial access vector in 22 percent of reviewed breaches and that password reuse remained common among affected users.

The article says fuzed identity can help organizations prioritize risk more accurately by distinguishing between low-risk exposure and cases involving privileges, reused credentials, active session cookies, or newly exposed accounts. It also applies the same idea to cybercrime, arguing that attribution can connect aliases, emails, devices, wallets, synthetic profiles, and other fragments into one actor. The article emphasizes that responsible programs must collect only security-relevant information, document purpose, retain provenance, restrict access, use confidence thresholds, and avoid employee surveillance.

  • An infostealer infection that starts from a personal activity such as a gaming download, personal email, browser extension, or pirated application can become an enterprise security incident if it captures corporate credentials or active session cookies.
  • Searching only for exposed corporate email addresses can miss meaningful risk because a personal email address, phone number, or home device may be linked to the same employee and to reusable access into business systems.
  • Two breach alerts that look similar at the account level may require very different responses once external context is added, such as whether the person has administrator privileges, reused credentials, or an active session cookie exposed from a personal device.
  • The article frames attribution as a way to collapse criminal fragmentation, because aliases, email addresses, phone numbers, devices, wallets, shell companies, and synthetic personas may appear independent until corroborating evidence links them to one actor.
  • The article draws a sharp operational boundary between security exposure reduction and employee surveillance, stating that identity intelligence should not be used to judge political opinions, personal relationships, lawful behavior, health matters, or other private-life details.

The article says work accounts and personal online accounts can no longer be treated as separate, because attackers already look at the whole person: home computers, personal email, phone numbers, saved logins, and work access. Employees, contractors, executives, suppliers, and companies are affected when a personal device or reused password gives criminals a path into business systems. It argues that companies need to connect only the security-relevant clues about a person’s online exposure so they can reduce real risks, while still respecting privacy and avoiding employee surveillance.

APTs Top the List of Most Active Threat Actors in H1 2026

Cyble’s H1 2026 threat landscape analysis tracked 261 active threat actor profiles worldwide, with nation-state APT groups making up the largest share at about 45%. Security teams should prioritize monitoring major active groups such as Bluenoroff, UNC6508, Volt Typhoon, Desert Falcons, and SideCopy.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs tracked 261 distinct threat actor profiles active worldwide between January and June 2026.
  • 02Nation-state Advanced Persistent Threat groups were the largest category, accounting for 118 profiles, or just over 45% of the total tracked profiles.
  • 03Ransomware operators accounted for 75 profiles, followed by 34 hacktivist collectives, 31 cybercriminal groups, and 3 extortion-only groups.
  • 04CRIL identified Bluenoroff, UNC6508, Volt Typhoon, Desert Falcons, and SideCopy as high-confidence, high-activity groups for security teams to track through the rest of 2026.
  • 05The article says Cyble Vision provides ongoing tracking of threat groups, including new actor emergence, changes in tactics, and targeting changes.

Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs analyzed the global threat landscape for the first half of 2026 across ransomware, initial access brokers, data breaches and leaks, nation-state espionage, hacktivism, and other activity. The analysis tracked 261 distinct threat actor profiles active worldwide between January and June. These profiles included identifiable groups and individuals operating across nation-state espionage, ransomware, hacktivism, and cybercrime.

Nation-state Advanced Persistent Threat groups were the largest category, with 118 profiles, or just over 45% of the total. Ransomware operators followed with 75 profiles, while hacktivist collectives accounted for 34, cybercriminal groups for 31, and extortion-only groups for 3. The article says the small extortion-only category indicates that pure extortion has largely been absorbed into ransomware, where double extortion is now part of the model.

CRIL highlighted Bluenoroff, UNC6508, Volt Typhoon, Desert Falcons, and SideCopy as high-confidence and highly active groups for security teams to track through the rest of 2026. Bluenoroff is described as impersonating crypto investors and placing malicious links in victims’ Calendly scheduling accounts, while Volt Typhoon uses “living off the land” methods to blend into normal network activity. UNC6508 is described as compromising externally accessible REDCap research environments, creating malicious mail-forwarding rules, and routing activity through US-based residential proxies and compromised routers to obscure attribution.

  • The article interprets the very small number of extortion-only groups as evidence that pure extortion has largely been absorbed into the ransomware business model, with double extortion becoming a standard ransomware practice.
  • The threat actor mix varies significantly by region, meaning a global ranking alone is not enough to understand which groups are most relevant to a specific organization or location.
  • Bluenoroff’s use of Calendly scheduling accounts shows that trusted everyday business tools can be abused as part of financially motivated social engineering campaigns against the cryptocurrency sector.

Cyble says it tracked 261 active online threat groups and individuals worldwide in the first half of 2026, with government-backed groups making up the largest share. These groups target areas such as cryptocurrency, financial services, education, healthcare, government, defense, communications, energy, manufacturing, media, and law enforcement across regions including the U.S., Canada, the Middle East, India, and Afghanistan. The broader concern is that many groups are operating at the same time, using trusted tools and hidden access methods to steal information, make money, or prepare for possible future disruption.

Inside Elastic InfoSec's agentic SOC: How we cut AI agent LLM calls by 60%

Elastic InfoSec reduced AI agent LLM calls by about 60% by measuring baseline usage, analyzing real conversation traces, replacing vague prompt budgets with concrete stopping checklists, and continuously monitoring for drift. The key lesson is that agent cost optimization is less about shortening prompts and more about controlling repeated LLM calls, redundant tool use, and inconsistent investigation paths.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Elastic InfoSec runs 14 AI agents in its security operations pipeline and found that some agents were making up to 19 LLM calls for work that needed about 8 calls.
  • 02Elastic reduced LLM call counts on the same workload to 7–9 by using a five-step optimization loop: measure the baseline, capture test conversations, analyze traces, revise and verify instructions, and monitor for drift.
  • 03The article says the dominant cost driver in an agentic workflow is the number of LLM calls, because each call carries the growing conversation history as input context.
  • 04Elastic found that vague instructions such as “Target 5–10 rounds” were less effective than concrete stopping checklists that tell the agent which steps to complete and when to emit a verdict.
  • 05The article recommends monitoring production agents after prompt changes because new alert types, detection rule changes, and data source changes can cause previously optimized agents to become inefficient again.

Elastic InfoSec describes how it optimized 14 AI agents used in its security operations pipeline after finding that they were producing correct verdicts but using more large language model calls than necessary. Some agents were taking up to 19 LLM calls for work that needed about 8, with thousands of input tokens per call. Using the same workload, Elastic reduced LLM call counts to 7–9 by applying a repeatable five-step optimization loop.

The article argues that agent optimization is different from prompt engineering because the main cost driver is not prompt length but the number of LLM calls and the growing conversation history carried into each call. Elastic’s process is to measure a baseline, capture representative test conversations, analyze conversation traces for inefficiency patterns, revise and verify instructions, and monitor for drift. The article highlights patterns such as redundant tool calls, schema exploration, excessive reasoning-only calls, wide default query ranges, and missing stopping criteria.

A key technical example is replacing vague instructions such as “Target 5–10 rounds” with a concrete ordered checklist that tells the agent which investigation steps to complete and when to emit a verdict. Elastic also recommends telling agents not to requery data already present in enrichment context and verifying changes in a QA environment before production deployment. After deployment, Elastic advises monitoring metrics such as average tokens, average LLM calls, maximum token spikes, and call-count variance so new alert types or data changes do not cause costs to drift upward again.

  • Trimming a system prompt may have limited cost impact because Elastic found that conversation history carried forward on each LLM call was the dominant token weight, with average input tokens per call ranging from about 10,000 to 36,000 depending on agent scope.
  • A numeric budget such as “Target 5–10 rounds” did not stop an agent from making 14–19 LLM calls, while replacing it with a named investigation checklist and an explicit instruction to emit a verdict reduced the same alert class to 7–9 calls.
  • Optimization scripts cannot automatically inspect conversations created by other users in Agent Builder because conversation bodies are per-user access-controlled and return 404 even for other roles, so Elastic recommends generating representative test conversations under the optimizer’s own credentials.
  • Run-to-run token variance is treated as a diagnostic signal, because a 2–3× spread on similar inputs indicates the agent is deciding its investigation path at runtime instead of following a consistent method.
  • Pre-enrichment can become wasteful unless the prompt explicitly tells the agent not to requery entities or fields already present in the starting context.

Elastic’s own security team found that its automated AI helpers were giving correct answers but were taking too many expensive steps to do so. The article explains the process they used to measure the problem, study what the AI helpers were doing, rewrite their instructions, and keep watching for the problem to return. This matters because teams using these tools at real-world scale can spend far more money than necessary if the AI keeps asking for more information or repeating work instead of stopping when it has enough.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-10818) WPForms Pro Arbitrary File Upload Leading to Remote Code Execution

WPForms Pro has a high-severity arbitrary file upload flaw, CVE-2026-10818, that can let unauthenticated attackers leave executable files on WordPress servers and potentially achieve remote code execution. Sites using public file upload forms should update to WPForms 2.0.0 or later and check upload directories for suspicious executable files.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-10818 is an arbitrary file upload vulnerability in WPForms Pro that affects versions up to and including 1.10.1.1 according to the CVE record.
  • 02The flaw is in the ajax_chunk_upload_finalize function, where validation happens after upload chunks and file contents have already been written to disk, and rejected files are not deleted.
  • 03An unauthenticated attacker can leave a chosen file in the WordPress uploads directory, which can lead to remote code execution if the web server executes that file.
  • 04The article says sites running affected WPForms Pro versions with public forms that include file upload fields are the main exposure concern.
  • 05WPForms version 2.0.0 includes a changelog entry matching the vulnerability behavior, and the article recommends treating anything below 2.0.0 as in scope until WPForms states otherwise.

CVE-2026-10818 is an arbitrary file upload vulnerability in WPForms Pro, the paid edition of a widely deployed WordPress form builder plugin. The flaw was published on July 25, 2026, with Wordfence as the assigning CNA, and carries a CVSS v3.1 base score of 8.1. The affected product is listed as WPForms Pro in versions up to and including 1.10.1.1, while WPForms Lite is not listed.

The vulnerability is in the ajax_chunk_upload_finalize function, which handles the final step of a chunked file upload. File type validation happens only after chunk metadata and file contents have already been written to disk, and the assembled file is not deleted when validation fails. As a result, an unauthenticated attacker can leave a file of their choosing in the WordPress uploads directory, and if the web server executes that file, the result is remote code execution.

The article emphasizes that exposure depends not only on version but also on whether a published form exposes a file upload field. It identifies marketing sites, campaign microsites, brand or product sites, press pages, and careers portals as common affected assets, and says Communication Services made up 62.1% of observed impacted assets in CyCognito’s data. WPForms released version 2.0.0 on July 14, 2026, with a changelog entry matching the described behavior, and the article recommends treating anything below 2.0.0 as in scope until WPForms states otherwise.

  • The article warns that teams should not rely strictly on the CVE’s affected-version range, because WPForms 1.10.2.x is outside the listed range but the vendor changelog suggests the relevant fix did not appear until 2.0.0.
  • Exposure triage should prioritize whether a public form has a file upload field, because the article distinguishes between a site merely running the affected plugin and a site exposing the vulnerable upload path.
  • The article highlights that the most exposed systems are often marketing, campaign, brand, press, or careers WordPress sites rather than core corporate applications, making ownership and inventory harder to manage.
  • Communication Services accounted for 62.1% of observed exposed assets in CyCognito’s data, which the article links to media organizations’ large numbers of WordPress publishing sites and frequent need to accept public file submissions.
  • The article recommends checking whether WordPress plugin auto-updates have already applied the fix before scheduling emergency work, since some sites may already be patched.

The article explains a flaw in WPForms Pro, a paid WordPress form plugin, that can let someone with no login place a file on a website through a public form upload feature, and in some cases that file could be run by the website server. The sites most affected are WordPress sites using WPForms Pro with public file upload forms, such as careers pages, media tip lines, campaign sites, and other pages that accept files from strangers. This matters because many organizations have lots of marketing or campaign WordPress sites that are hard to track, so a simple form feature can become a way for outsiders to take control of a server if it is not updated and checked.

The article reports a specific high-severity WPForms Pro vulnerability that can allow unauthenticated arbitrary file upload and possible remote code execution on WordPress sites with public upload forms. It is broadly relevant because affected assets may include many marketing, campaign, media, and careers sites, and the article provides concrete patching and triage guidance.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-60358) Oracle Access Manager Takeover via Authentication Engine

Oracle patched CVE-2026-60358, a critical pre-authentication Oracle Access Manager flaw that can let an unauthenticated attacker take over the authentication broker and potentially affect all applications trusting it. Organizations should urgently verify patch coverage, restrict exposed Access Manager endpoints where possible, and review logs and trust secrets after remediation.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-60358 is a critical vulnerability in the Authentication Engine component of Oracle Access Manager with a CVSS v3.1 base score of 10.0.
  • 02Oracle describes the flaw as easily exploitable by an unauthenticated attacker with network access over HTTP, with no user interaction or credentials required.
  • 03Oracle Access Manager versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0 are the affected supported versions, and earlier unsupported releases are likely affected without receiving patches.
  • 04Oracle addressed CVE-2026-60358 in the July 2026 Critical Patch Update released on July 21, 2026.
  • 05The article recommends inventorying internet-facing Oracle Access Manager instances, restricting HTTP access where possible, reviewing logs, auditing administrative changes, rotating credentials and federation trust secrets after remediation, and treating applications that trust Access Manager sessions as in scope.

Oracle disclosed CVE-2026-60358 on July 21, 2026 as part of the July 2026 Critical Patch Update. The flaw affects the Authentication Engine component of Oracle Access Manager, the single sign-on product in the Oracle Fusion Middleware stack. Oracle assigned it a CVSS v3.1 base score of 10.0 and describes it as exploitable before authentication by an unauthenticated attacker with network access over HTTP.

A successful attack can result in takeover of Oracle Access Manager, which matters because Access Manager issues and validates sessions that other applications trust. Oracle states that attacks may significantly impact products beyond Access Manager itself, and the article explains that the blast radius can include systems sitting behind the login service. At the time of writing, Oracle had not published root cause details, and there was no public exploit code or confirmed exploitation in the wild.

The affected supported versions are Oracle Access Manager 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0, while earlier unsupported releases are likely affected but do not receive patches. The article says exposed Access Manager assets commonly appear as web-facing login endpoints for supplier, procurement, dealer, partner, customer self-service, and ERP environments, with exposure concentrated in energy and automotive and a smaller presence in banking. Recommended actions include inventorying internet-facing instances, restricting HTTP access where possible, reviewing logs for suspicious sessions, auditing administrative changes, rotating service account credentials and federation trust secrets after remediation, and treating applications that trust Access Manager sessions as in scope.

  • The article emphasizes that the real blast radius is not limited to Oracle Access Manager itself because applications behind it trust the sessions it issues and validates.
  • The affected assets are often internet-facing by design, so taking them offline can also make every application behind the login service unavailable to external users.
  • Exposure in the article’s data is concentrated in energy and automotive organizations, with a smaller presence in banking, particularly around supplier, procurement, dealer, and SSO portals.
  • The July 2026 Critical Patch Update contains 1,449 new security patches, so teams should specifically verify that their Fusion Middleware patching covers CVE-2026-60358 rather than assuming it does.
  • Organizations on unsupported Access Manager versions cannot rely on a patch for this issue and should assume exposure because Oracle says earlier releases are likely affected but are not receiving fixes.

Oracle disclosed and patched a very serious flaw in Oracle Access Manager, a product many organizations use as the front door for logging in to business websites. The affected systems are web-facing login pages, often used for supplier portals, dealer systems, customer self-service sites, and ERP front ends, especially in energy, automotive, and some banking environments. If attackers took over this login system, they could make other connected applications believe they were legitimate users, so the risk goes beyond one server and could affect many business systems behind it.

Nuxt released security updates for multiple vulnerabilities affecting Nuxt 3.x and 4.x, along with a separate critical development-only vulnerability in @nuxt/devtools. Nuxt 4.5.1 and 3.21.10 address issues including server-side remote code execution, authorization bypass, denial of service, and cross-user payload disclosure. @nuxt/devtools 3.3.1 fixes a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting development servers.

The most serious production issue, GHSA-9473-5f9j-94wq, can enable server-side remote code execution through server island props. It requires vue.runtimeCompiler to be enabled, which is off by default, and an application pattern where attacker-controlled island props reach Vue’s dynamic component resolution. A related vulnerability, GHSA-48hr-524c-v5w3, can allow unauthorized instantiation of HTML elements or globally registered components through server island props, but does not enable code execution.

Socket has published free Certified Patches for GHSA-9473-5f9j-94wq and GHSA-48hr-524c-v5w3, and is preparing patches for the remaining Nuxt advisories. Nuxt recommends upgrading to Nuxt 4.5.1 or 3.21.10 and refreshing lockfiles to ensure @nuxt/devtools@3.3.1 or later is resolved. Teams using authenticated pages with Nuxt cache, swr, or isr route rules should purge CDN and edge caches after upgrading because previously cached _payload.json responses may remain available until explicitly evicted.

  • The highest-severity production remote code execution issue requires vue.runtimeCompiler to be enabled, which is not the default, and also depends on attacker-controlled server island props reaching Vue dynamic component resolution.
  • The Nuxt DevTools remote code execution issue is limited to development environments, but it can still be reached through another local process, an exposed dev server on the local network, or a malicious site visited while the dev server is running.
  • Upgrading alone may not fully remove exposure for authenticated pages using Nuxt cache, swr, or isr route rules because previously cached _payload.json responses can remain available until CDN and edge caches are purged.
  • The route-rule authorization bypass specifically involves appMiddleware used with route rules containing uppercase characters, making route-rule key casing an actionable review target.

Nuxt released fixes for several security problems in Nuxt 3.x and 4.x, plus a separate serious problem in @nuxt/devtools used during development. Organizations using affected Nuxt versions could face risks such as attackers running code on a server, bypassing access checks, causing outages, or exposing cached page data between users. The article says users should upgrade to Nuxt 4.5.1 or 3.21.10 and @nuxt/devtools 3.3.1, or use Socket’s free patches if they cannot upgrade right away.

It also notes the security argument that closed models can create single points of failure, while acknowledging limits: once weights are released they cannot be recalled, modified versions are hard to trace, and open models still trail the best closed ones in some areas important to defenders.

  • The article frames model access as a business continuity issue, arguing that losing a closed AI service can be more like losing critical infrastructure than losing a convenience tool.
  • The security argument for open weights is defensive rather than purely philosophical: defenders may need models with comparable capabilities to attackers in order to test, simulate, and respond.
  • The letter’s security case is limited by the fact that released model weights cannot be recalled and modified versions are hard to trace.

Major technology companies including NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, Google, IBM, Mistral, Hugging Face, Mozilla, and the Linux Foundation signed a letter urging the U.S. government not to restrict AI models that people and companies can download and run themselves. The article says this matters because a recent closed AI model from Anthropic was pulled offline worldwide after a U.S. government order, showing that businesses relying on someone else’s AI service can lose access suddenly. Helpdesk Hijackers: Teams Vishing, Quick Assist, and GoGRPC Backdoor

Zscaler ThreatLabz reports a likely ransomware initial-access broker using Microsoft Teams vishing and Quick Assist to compromise organizations, then deploying the evolving GoGRPC backdoor and related proxy/exfiltration tools. The campaigns have grown more sophisticated and selective, with recent activity focused on corporate environments and tooling such as Kind, RevSocket, PyGRPC, S3Siphon, and RSOX.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Zscaler ThreatLabz has tracked attacks since January 2026 from a threat actor that likely acts as an initial access broker for ransomware attacks.
  • 02The attacks begin with vishing through Microsoft Teams, where the threat actor poses as IT or helpdesk staff and persuades victims to launch a Quick Assist remote support session.
  • 03After initial access, the threat actor uses PowerShell scripts to collect host information, establish persistence, and deploy the Go-based GoGRPC backdoor or other malware tools.
  • 04ThreatLabz identified four GoGRPC variants named Lep, Giver, Pet, and Kind, with overlapping capabilities and implementation differences including TLS support, fingerprinting behavior, and obfuscation.
  • 05The threat actor has also deployed tools named BlindDoor, RevSocket, PyGRPC, S3Siphon, and RSOX for backdoor access, proxying, reconnaissance, and file exfiltration.

Zscaler ThreatLabz has been tracking attacks since January 2026 from a threat actor that is likely an initial access broker for ransomware attacks. The campaigns begin with targeted vishing through Microsoft Teams, where the actor poses as IT or helpdesk staff and persuades the victim to launch a Quick Assist remote support session. After gaining access, the actor uses PowerShell scripts to gather host information, create persistence, and deploy malware tools.

The main malware examined in the article is GoGRPC, a Go-based backdoor with four observed variants named Lep, Giver, Pet, and Kind. These variants share overlapping capabilities but differ in areas such as fingerprinting, agent ID generation, mutex checks, obfuscation, TLS support, and gRPC protocol details. GoGRPC communicates with its command-and-control server using gRPC over HTTP/2, with later variants adding TLS support and the Kind variant changing the endpoint to /Refuse/Connect.

ThreatLabz also observed additional tools deployed in these campaigns, including BlindDoor, S3Siphon, RevSocket, PyGRPC, and RSOX. These tools provide functions such as command execution, file exfiltration to an AWS S3 bucket, and SOCKS proxy tunneling over gRPC or WebSockets. The article states that recent activity has become more selective, using PowerShell scripts to assess antivirus and endpoint detection tools, domain controllers, and corporate environment characteristics before further payload deployment.

  • GoGRPC uses gRPC over HTTP/2 directly for command-and-control communications, which the article notes is unlike common public C2 frameworks where gRPC is typically used only for internal communication between framework components.
  • The Lep and Giver variants communicated over port 443 without TLS, while the later Pet and Kind variants added TLS support, showing a concrete shift toward more protected network traffic.
  • Recent activity became more selective, with PowerShell scripts used to assess antivirus, endpoint detection, domain controller presence, and broader corporate environment value before deploying later-stage payloads.
  • S3Siphon is designed to avoid many system and temporary files while targeting common user folders such as Desktop, Documents, Downloads, OneDrive, Pictures, and Videos, indicating file theft focused on user data rather than indiscriminate collection.
  • RSOX can take its server URL and authentication token from environment variables instead of only using hardcoded values, allowing the threat actor to reconfigure infrastructure without changing the binary.

The article describes a group that tricks employees through Microsoft Teams by pretending to be IT helpdesk staff, then convinces them to start a Quick Assist remote support session. Once inside, the group installs tools that can collect information, run commands, move traffic through the victim’s computer, and steal files. This affects organizations targeted by these calls, especially corporate environments, and matters because the activity appears connected to preparing for ransomware attacks and possible extortion.

agentic concept

AI models concept
